lesson.title: Deciding with data
lesson.subtitle: Lead a data question at school

video.title: Deciding with data: Lead a data question at school
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello - primary teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Narrator - the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Our staff wanted to move the start of the school day later. Some said pupils would sleep more and learn better. Others worried about parents' work. How could data help us decide?
Today: how a school can use data to decide well, and when data is not enough.
Data cannot make a decision for you. It shows what is likely to happen and to whom. People still weigh what matters most, and they own the decision.

We wrote one clear question: if we start thirty minutes later, will lateness and tiredness fall? Then we chose what to measure before collecting anything, so we could not pick the numbers we liked afterwards.
Two classes started later for six weeks while two similar classes did not. Late arrivals per week fell from twelve to five in the trial classes, and barely changed in the others.
Numbers were only half the story. We also asked parents and pupils, and some families could not manage the later finish. Their voices changed our plan more than any chart.
Ms Farah shared the results with everyone, including what did not work. Now any teacher can bring a question to our monthly data meeting. Small honest trials have become how our school decides.
Quick check! Why did we keep two similar classes on the old start time during the trial?
To compare fairly. Lateness might have fallen anyway, because of the weather or the season. The other classes show what would have happened without the change.
In the app, open the decision lab. Weigh the evidence and the voices for a school change, and see how your choice affects each group.
Your turn. The data shows a later start cuts lateness. Who should make the final decision?
The school's people, using the data and the voices together. Remember: ask one clear question, run a fair trial, listen as well as count, and share what you find.
Try it with your staff this week: bring one school question to your next meeting and agree on what to measure. Then plan a small trial, with a similar group kept the same for a fair comparison.

checkpoints.prompt: Why did we keep two similar classes on the old start time during the trial?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: they show what would have happened without the change.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: without a comparison group, a fall in lateness could be chance or the season.
